# DocStory

> First-hand interviews with medical students about what their schools are really like: 54 interviews covering 44 U.S. medical schools (40 MD, 4 DO). Each school page pairs the interviews with figures from the school's own published class profile and cost of attendance and, where available, U.S. government data (NIH research funding, ClinicalTrials.gov, CMS hospital data, Census rent). Run since 2017 by people who were medical students at UC Irvine, Creighton, and the John A. Burns School of Medicine.

Interviews are written by the students themselves, mostly in answer to a standard set of questions (typical day, curriculum, culture, clinical training, advice for applicants), and are edited only for typos and obvious grammar. Each interview reflects one student's experience in the year it was written; the publication date is shown on the interview page. School pages list the official sources for their figures.

## Interviews

- [Ana Khatia — Albany Medical College](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/albany-medical-college/ana-khatia/) (MS2, 2022): Ana describes days built around Anki reviews in the morning and new material after lunch, with first-year lectures delivered online and instructors quick to hop on a Zoom call to help. Ana calls the class culture “we are all in this together,” and says the school was extremely accommodating during family emergencies in first year. Albany suits outdoorsy students, with hiking, skiing and drives to Boston or New York, though the winters are brutal and the nightlife is limited.
- [Justin — Baylor College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/baylor-college-of-medicine/justin/) (MS1, 2019): Justin describes four 50-minute lectures each morning, afternoon classes until 4, and daily Anki review using student-made decks for lecture material. Justin calls the class collaborative, with block parties as the best part of each term, and lists older students’ help, expert professors, low tuition and the Texas Medical Center setting as strengths.
- [Michele Cabeza — Baylor College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/baylor-college-of-medicine/michele-cabeza/) (MS1, 2018): Michele lays out Baylor’s week in detail: recorded morning lectures, anatomy lab and a group problem-solving course in the afternoons, and a Patient, Physician, and Society course that pairs each student with a community preceptor. The preclinical curriculum is only 1.5 years and true pass/fail, which Michele credits for a collaborative culture, helped by a Peer Resource Network of older students who mentor each first-year group. Faculty reach out personally when a student’s exam scores fall well below average.
- [Anonymous — Brody School of Medicine at East Carolina University](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/brody-school-of-medicine/anonymous-ms3/) (MS3, 2022): This third-year student describes rotation days at ECU Health Medical Center, the school’s main teaching hospital, which is connected to the school building by a hallway. With about 80 students per class, everyone recognizes each other and the culture leans collaborative; each year second-years chalk encouraging messages on the sidewalk the night before the first-years’ first exam. Greenville is small but rent is very cheap, and preclinical grading had just moved to pass/fail while clerkships still used letter grades.
- [Bao Vu — California University of Science and Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/california-university-of-science-and-medicine/bao-vu/) (MS1, 2020): Bao describes a flipped classroom at a new school, with class only three days a week and the rest of the week for self-study with Boards and Beyond, Pathoma, Sketchy and Anki. Because the school was new, students had real say: Bao notes that they helped change grading from letter grades to pass/fail and the schedule from five days a week to three. Bao applied twice before being admitted and advises applicants to be themselves in interviews instead of saying what interviewers want to hear.
- [Allison Martin — Chicago Medical School at Rosalind Franklin University](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/rosalind-franklin-university/allison-martin/) (MS2, 2018): Allison, a night owl who skips lecture, studies with recorded lectures, Pathoma and Sketchy at double speed late into the night. Allison chose Chicago Medical School for its supportive, collaborative culture, where students show up for each other’s fundraisers and talks and rally around classmates having a hard time. With no single affiliated hospital, students rotate through most hospitals in the Chicago area, which Allison sees as a plus; the first two years are spent in quiet North Chicago.
- [Drew Weinstein — Chicago Medical School at Rosalind Franklin University](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/rosalind-franklin-university/drew-weinstein/) (MS2, 2018): Drew describes a structured day from 7:30am in the library through lectures, labs and evening study, using Anki every day because cramming does not work. Instructors rarely take questions during class but are approachable afterward, and Drew says none of them are looking to fail anyone. The campus is quiet and good for studying, 45 minutes by train from Chicago, and Drew advises applying early and broadly and practicing interview skills.
- [Eric Nguyen — Creighton University School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/creighton-university-school-of-medicine/eric-nguyen/) (MS2, 2018): Eric describes streaming lectures and studying with active recall and spaced repetition, and found Creighton’s faculty unusually available, often answering emails within hours. Eric highlights the school’s Jesuit identity, including Wisdom Groups where students meet with a Jesuit to reflect on meaning in medicine, and teaching that stresses how illness affects a patient’s whole life. Omaha is welcoming and diverse with good food, though Eric misses hiking and finds other major cities a long drive away.
- [Tim Ellis-Caleo — David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/ucla-geffen-school-of-medicine/tim-ellis-caleo/) (MS4, 2018): Tim, a fourth-year, describes a pass/fail preclinical curriculum in organ-system blocks with two hours of lecture a day, weekly problem-based learning and a longitudinal preceptorship, followed by a traditional core clerkship year. Tim argues that preclinical curriculum details matter less than they seem, and that UCLA’s real strength is clinical training across many sites with residents and faculty who give students real responsibility. Tim relied almost entirely on Anki and urges applicants to ask how much responsibility third-year students get.
- [Jonathan Acosta — Drexel University College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/drexel-university-college-of-medicine/jonathan-acosta/) (MS2, 2018): Jonathan describes long, self-directed study days: all lectures are podcasted, so Jonathan studies on campus from 6am to about 7pm and then reviews material with a study group of three friends. The class atmosphere is very non-competitive, and Jonathan valued Drexel teaching the business side of health care, from legislation to insurance and reimbursement. Jonathan advises premeds to choose a school by its people and to expect secondary applications to take a lot of time.
- [Alex — Duke University School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/duke-university-school-of-medicine/alex/) (MS2, 2018): Alex, a former English major who did a post-bacc, describes Duke’s minimal mandatory class time and recorded lectures, with plenty of independent study and a weekly three-hour Clinical Skills Foundation class. Duke’s condensed preclinical curriculum puts students on the wards in second year, which opens with a three-week Clinical Skills Intensive. Alex chose Duke because its students seemed among the happiest on the interview trail, and Durham’s low cost of living let Alex borrow less than offered.
- [Rossen Kirkov — Eastern Virginia Medical School](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/eastern-virginia-medical-school/rossen-kirkov/) (MS3, 2018): Rossen stopped going to lecture in the second semester and prepared for Step 1 with First Aid, Pathoma and UWorld, and walks through the trade-offs of the common study methods. EVMS is very community-service oriented, with the student-run HOPES clinic for underserved patients and no sense of competition between classmates. Rossen points to clinical training at Sentara Norfolk General, a Level 1 trauma center, and a strong ultrasound program as strengths.
- [Anonymous — Florida State University College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/florida-state-university-college-of-medicine/anonymous-ms3/) (MS3, 2019): This student describes a first year that starts in early June with a summer of full-body dissection, and learning communities: four shared spaces with kitchens and study rooms that split each class into groups of about 30 from the first day. Preclinical grading is true pass/fail with no ranking, and students rotate with community physicians starting in the spring of first year. For third and fourth year the class splits up across regional campuses around Florida, which means mostly one-on-one work with physicians, but also saying goodbye to friends.
- [Abraham Cheloff — Harvard Medical School](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/harvard-medical-school/abraham-cheloff/) (MS2, 2020): Abraham describes Harvard's 14-month preclinical phase, taught as a flipped classroom: students prepare with videos the night before, then work through cases in small groups each morning, with Wednesdays spent at a clinical site. Grading was pass/fail with no class ranking, which Abraham credits for a collaborative culture, and the weekly clinical days left Abraham feeling well prepared for the clerkship year. Even in the clinical year, each rotation includes a set number of “flex” afternoons off for appointments and other must-do tasks.
- [Austin Wininger — Indiana University School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/indiana-university-school-of-medicine/austin-wininger/) (MS3, 2018): Austin focuses on the clinical years: IU’s eight core clerkships, honors/high pass/pass grading driven mostly by clinical evaluations and NBME shelf exams, and studying with Online MedEd and UWorld. Austin found the jump to third year the hardest adjustment and advises asking preceptors directly for feedback and using the time after being dismissed to study. IU’s nine campuses across Indiana, plus county, children’s and VA hospitals in Indianapolis, offer both community and Level 1 trauma settings.
- [Will Tobolowsky — Johns Hopkins School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/johns-hopkins-school-of-medicine/will-tobolowsky/) (MS3, 2018): Will describes preclinical days of three to six lectures plus small groups, with one course taught at a time in two- to four-week blocks and a weekly afternoon at an outpatient clinic. Will found more events and opportunities than time and suggests picking a few to stick with. Will is candid about crime in East Baltimore but argues that hospitals in such areas expose students to a wider range of serious cases, and recommends Sketchy, Pathoma, First Aid, USMLE Rx and UWorld.
- [Jeremy Storck — Kentucky College of Osteopathic Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/kentucky-college-of-osteopathic-medicine/jeremy-storck/) (OMS3, 2018): Jeremy describes lecture-heavy days in a single classroom, four-week blocks between exams, and studying with Anki, Pathoma, Sketchy and especially Boards and Beyond. KYCOM’s mission is training primary care physicians for underserved areas, and Pikeville, a town of about 6,000 in Eastern Kentucky’s coal country, offers outdoor life, friendly people and early chances to serve the community. Jeremy advises applicants to choose schools whose missions match their goals instead of applying to dozens, and looks forward each April to Hillbilly Days, a four-day festival that takes over the town and gives students the time off.
- [Arya Shah — Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/mayo-clinic-school-of-medicine/arya-shah/) (MS4, 2018): Arya, a fourth-year who settled on psychiatry, describes a lecture-based first year, a second year of systems lectures and hospital-based doctoring groups, and clerkships after that. With only 40 to 50 students per class, Arya knows every classmate, and every faculty member, mentor and preceptor, by name, in a small town built around a large academic medical center. Arya found that food, exercise, sleep and hobbies matter as much as studying, and advises premeds to make time for the humanities.
- [Catherine Boatman — Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/medical-college-of-georgia/catherine-boatman/) (MS2, 2019): Catherine starts studying at 6:30am, attends every lecture while making Anki cards, and studies into the evening, with Brazilian Jiu Jitsu as a break. MCG’s Academic House System splits a class of more than 200 into 13 houses, each with its own apartment-style space in the medical school building, outings paid for by the school and an end-of-year House Olympics; Catherine calls it a leading reason for choosing MCG. Catherine took six gap years before medical school and would not change a thing.
- [Austin Dopp — Medical College of Wisconsin](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/medical-college-of-wisconsin/austin-dopp/) (MS2, 2018): Austin, who is married with three children, describes a day of morning lectures, afternoon study or research, family time from 5 to 7, and more studying after the kids are in bed. Lectures are recorded, and in a class of about 200 Austin finds the culture very supportive, with classmates constantly sharing tips and study aids. Austin values the school’s ties to the Kern Institute and a weekly Clinical Apprenticeship with a physician, while doubting how meaningful early patient contact is before the first two years are done.
- [Dani Sychowski — Midwestern University Chicago College of Osteopathic Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/midwestern-chicago-college-of-osteopathic-medicine/dani-sychowski/) (OMS1, 2023): Dani describes CCOM’s symptoms-based curriculum, where each week centers on one symptom that ties together lectures, anatomy, OMM and physical exam labs; Dani found it works well some weeks and less well others. Preclinical courses use A-through-C letter grades, but the class of about 200 is collaborative, sharing notes in group chats, and second-years mentor first-years through a big-little program. The campus is in suburban Downers Grove, next to a forest preserve and an easy trip into Chicago, and Dani valued living on campus about 45 minutes from family.
- [Nick Bacher — New York Medical College](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/new-york-medical-college/nick-bacher/) (MS3, 2018): Nick describes regimented first-year days giving way to mostly self-study in second year, with exceptionally good standardized patients and an emergency department preceptorship as clinical highlights. Nick pushes back on the idea that schools without pass/fail preclinical grading are competitive, saying that has never been the case at NYMC, and chose the school for its sense of community. The campus is in suburban Westchester County, just over half an hour by train from Manhattan, and Nick advises premeds to be their own advocate instead of relying only on pre-health advisors.
- [Regine Goh — Northwestern Feinberg School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/northwestern-feinberg-school-of-medicine/regine-goh/) (MS3, 2018): Regine describes third-year days that vary by rotation, after first two years that mixed lectures with problem-based learning in small groups. From the start of medical school, students spend time twice a month in preceptorships and education-centered medical homes, primary care clinics where students from all four years work together. Regine, from California, loves living in Chicago without it being prohibitively expensive, volunteered at student-run free clinics around the city, and recommends the student sketch comedy show In Vivo.
- [Emily He — Rush Medical College](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/rush-medical-college/emily-he/) (MS1, 2018): Emily describes Rush’s flipped classroom with no lectures: students work through self-study packets built around a patient case, take a quiz at 8am, then apply the material in classes of 16 to 17. Hands-on patient care started in the third week of school, with a different clinical placement each semester, and monthly interprofessional sessions put medical students in small groups with nursing, therapy and other health students. Emily, who moved from Southern California, gets around Chicago easily on the students’ unlimited transit pass and enjoys walking to Bulls games, since Rush is the team’s official health care provider.
- [Jonathan Carnino — School not given](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/misc/jonathan-carnino/) (MS1, 2023): Jonathan focuses on research: landing a paid undergraduate lab position by emailing several investigators at once, what makes a good research mentor, and why clinical research fits a medical student’s schedule better than basic science. At Boston University School of Medicine, Jonathan describes fully pass/fail preclinical courses with no ranking, LEADS weeks devoted to social determinants of health, and interviewing hospital patients just weeks into first year. Jonathan was a reapplicant and calls the two years spent working in biotech the best thing that could have happened.
- [Alexander Worix — Southern Illinois University School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/southern-illinois-university-school-of-medicine/alexander-worix/) (MS2, 2018): Alexander describes SIU’s problem-based learning, built around three-hour tutor groups where five to eight students work through virtual patient cases and teach each other the underlying science. Clinical skills start in the first week, with standardized patients, Clinical Competency Exams and, by the end of first year, a full head-to-toe physical exam to finish in under 45 minutes. Alexander chose SIU partly on cost, about half the yearly price of an out-of-state option, and notes that first year is in Carbondale before the class moves to Springfield.
- [Kyung Park — TCU Burnett School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/tcu-burnett-school-of-medicine/kyung-park/) (MS2, 2022): Kyung describes a pass/fail first phase with in-person application sessions most mornings and plenty of open “white space,” plus a longitudinal clerkship with a family or internal medicine preceptor from first year. With a class of 60, students belong to one of six houses, each with two faculty coaches who check in after exams and give career advice, and every student completes a research thesis to graduate. When inpatient work starts, students get 10 weeks of immersion rotations with feedback but no grades.
- [Caleb — Texas A&M University Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/texas-a-and-m-college-of-medicine/caleb/) (MS3, 2022): Caleb is in EnMed, Texas A&M’s combined engineering and medicine program in Houston, with a cohort of just 34 students that Caleb says feels like a family, for better and worse. Caleb describes a flipped-classroom preclerkship, Practice of Medicine courses that build to a weekly half-day preceptorship, and clerkship days that start at 6:30am at Houston Methodist. The program acted quickly on student feedback, moving to true pass/fail, unranked preclerkship grading and cutting the number of mandatory sessions.
- [Brittany Stelmar — Touro College of Osteopathic Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/touro-college-of-osteopathic-medicine/brittany-stelmar/) (OMS2, 2018): Brittany describes Touro’s Middletown campus, where students watch lecture videos beforehand and answer clicker questions in mandatory classes; Brittany likes the format but wishes the assigned videos were shorter and attendance optional. Professors email to set up tutoring whenever a student gets a subpar test grade. Working as an ER technician alongside DOs changed Brittany’s view of osteopathic medicine, and Brittany values the quiet small town, about an hour by train or bus from New York City.
- [Wei Ming Liang — Touro College of Osteopathic Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/touro-college-of-osteopathic-medicine/wei-ming-liang/) (OMS2, 2023): Wei Ming studies at Touro’s Harlem campus and lives at home with family in New York City, with a brother also in medical school. The curriculum is a flipped classroom with clicker questions in class, A-to-F grades and mostly mandatory attendance in first year, and Wei Ming finds OMM useful for building palpation skills while questioning some of its topics. Each student gets an upperclassman mentor and a faculty advisor, and Wei Ming highlights a twice-yearly health fair in Harlem and MedAchieve, a weekly mentoring program for high school students.
- [David — Tulane University School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/tulane-university-school-of-medicine/david/) (MS2, 2018): David studies at home most days, pairing Step 1 resources like Pathoma, Sketchy and First Aid with school lectures at double speed, for six to eight hours including breaks. David says the class itself is Tulane’s best feature: a diverse group with plenty of community programming, from volunteering at clinics to fundraising concerts. Clinical preparation includes monthly standardized patients, a simulation center, preceptors in the first two years and student-run clinics, and New Orleans is full of festivals and restaurants, though getting around without a car is hard.
- [Emily Hayward — UAB Heersink School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/university-of-alabama-birmingham/emily-hayward/) (MS3 (MD/PhD), 2018): Emily, an MD/PhD student in UAB’s Medical Scientist Training Program, describes Introduction to Clinical Medicine, which pairs groups of six students with one physician preceptor for two years and teaches each physical exam alongside the matching organ module. Within the first two weeks of school, Emily was taking vital signs and interviewing patients at Equal Access Birmingham, the student-run free clinic. Birmingham’s low cost of living stretches the MD/PhD stipend: many of Emily’s peers bought houses near campus, and Emily rents a whole house five minutes away.
- [Alexa Lucas — UC Irvine School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/uc-irvine-school-of-medicine/alexa-lucas/) (MS1, 2018): Alexa podcasts most lectures from coffee shops and keeps up with the pace by trading quick typed study guides for friends’ flashcards. UCI teaches the normal function of every system in first year and the pathology of every system in second, which Alexa likes as a way to see each system twice before boards. Alexa helps lead a global health and ultrasound education trip to Tanzania and a mentorship program for underserved high school girls, and decompresses at Orange County’s beaches and with an annual Disneyland pass.
- [Arnie Shah — UC Irvine School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/uc-irvine-school-of-medicine/arnie-shah/) (MS1, 2018): Arnie studies mostly from libraries and coffee shops and, with pass/no-pass classes, has learned to prioritize high-yield material and read clinical cases to make facts stick. Arnie describes a collaborative class that feels like family, with whole-class activities and an administration that asks for feedback and acts on it promptly. Arnie contributes to PLEXUS, UCI’s medical humanities journal, and warns that following application threads on Student Doctor Network made the gap year more stressful.
- [Steven Tohmasi — UC Irvine School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/uc-irvine-school-of-medicine/steven-tohmasi/) (MS2, 2018): Steven describes morning basic science classes, recorded lectures and a weekly three-hour small group in clinical foundations, ultrasound or simulation. UCI is a leader in ultrasound education: each year 30 to 40 students spend the summer after first year teaching point-of-care ultrasound abroad, and Steven’s team was headed to the University of Basel in Switzerland. The PACE program puts first- and second-years in clinic with a preceptor one half-day a week, and the campus is less than 15 minutes from the ocean.
- [Neela — UC San Diego School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/uc-san-diego-school-of-medicine/neela/) (MS1, 2018): Neela videocasts the optional 8am lectures at 1.5x speed and saves in-person time for small-group problem-based learning and Practice of Medicine, with pass/fail grading keeping stress low. Neela chose UCSD because its first-years seemed far happier than expected, and advises applicants to weigh student happiness over rankings. UCSD’s Free Clinic involves almost every student, and Neela helps manage its neurology and psychiatry clinics, seeing patients and presenting to attendings.
- [Prithwijit Roychowdhury — UMass Chan Medical School](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/university-of-massachusetts-medical-school/prithwijit-roychowdhury/) (MS2, 2018): Prithwijit describes days built around Anki, with afternoon classes in between, and relies on the Zanki deck, Sketchy, Pathoma and First Aid; Prithwijit’s one regret is not adopting Anki sooner. The culture is positive and supportive, starting with a first-year orientation camping trip run with second-years and continuing with social events where faculty and students mix. Worcester has distinct neighborhoods, new restaurants and a low cost of living, though public transportation is weak.
- [Priya Sorab — University of Cincinnati College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/university-of-cincinnati-college-of-medicine/priya-sorab/) (MS2, 2018): Priya describes mornings of mostly optional classes and varied afternoons: weekly Learning Community case and ethics discussions with 12 to 13 students and a physician, clinical skills sessions, and seeing patients at a doctor’s office every other week starting in first year. With about 170 students per class, Priya gets to know classmates well, and recommends First Aid, Pathoma and Sketchy. The campus has a college-town feel, with downtown Cincinnati nearby for restaurants and outings after exams.
- [Anonymous — University of Florida College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/university-of-florida-college-of-medicine/anonymous-ms2/) (MS2, 2019): This student describes 50-minute lectures, many recorded and optional, plus weekly three-hour Collaborative Learning Groups covering wellness, ethics, interviewing and feedback on write-ups, with dissection starting in the second semester. Students see real patients under their small-group leader from the second semester of first year, complete three preceptorships and can volunteer at the Equal Access Clinic. Gainesville is a college town where football game days transform campus, and clinical rotations also run in an urban setting in Jacksonville.
- [Gabriel Conley — University of Iowa Carver College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/university-of-iowa-carver-college-of-medicine/gabriel-conley/) (MS2, 2018): Gabriel describes Iowa’s fast-paced new curriculum, with exams every other Friday, core clerkships starting half a year earlier than at most schools, and Step 1 taken at the two-and-a-half-year mark. The culture is collaborative, with classmate tutors, shared notes and Carverpedia, a student-built wiki of study guides, plus a spring variety show put on by every class. Students can take a funded research fellowship of nearly $6,000 the summer after first year or pursue global health projects abroad, and Gabriel, an economics major, found that diagramming lectures works best.
- [Todd Jackson — University of Miami Miller School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/university-of-miami-miller-school-of-medicine/todd-jackson/) (MS3, 2018): Todd describes problem-based learning in groups of seven or eight with a faculty member, optional lectures, and third-year internal medicine days that run from 7am pre-rounding to about 5pm. Todd calls the culture laid back, highlighted by the Dean’s Cup, where medical students compete against UM law students in everything from flag football to baking. Todd sees Miami’s greatest strength as training with a diverse population, including many uninsured migrants from the Caribbean and South America who rely on UM and its partners for care.
- [Zach Donato — University of Miami Miller School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/university-of-miami-miller-school-of-medicine/zach-donato/) (MS2, 2022): Zach describes Miami’s NextGen curriculum, which moved clerkships into second year after a preclinical year of flipped-classroom, case-based learning organized by symptom. More than 70% of students take part in DOCS, a student-run clinic that holds health fairs in underserved neighborhoods roughly every month, and students train at Jackson and the University of Miami hospitals. Most students live in Brickell or downtown, which Zach compares to a mini New York City, though it is expensive.
- [Wilson Hoyt — University of Oklahoma College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/university-of-oklahoma-college-of-medicine/wilson-hoyt/) (MS1, 2022): Wilson describes OU’s module system, which places 15 to 17 students in a mod with its own swipe-access room, desks and lockers for the first two years, and calls the student culture one of the school’s best features. Clinical medicine courses run through the preclinical years, starting in week one with exam skills, ultrasound and X-ray, and students can book time in a simulation center with standardized patients. Grading is pass/fail with quartile rankings, and the area right around campus is a food desert, though downtown Oklahoma City nearby has affordable food and nightlife.
- [Jay Patel — University of Tennessee Health Science Center College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/ut-health-science-center/jay-patel/) (MS1, 2018): Jay describes morning classes followed by mandatory afternoon sessions such as ultrasound practice and a Principles of Medicine course, then studying on campus until 8 or 9pm. After pulling three all-nighters for the first exam, Jay switched to spaced repetition with classmates’ shared Quizlet and Anki sets, and credits SASSI, the student support center, for workshops on time management and wellbeing. The school sits in the Memphis Medical District alongside dentistry, pharmacy and PA programs, and Jay found Memphis vibrant without the traffic of bigger cities.
- [Dominic Carusillo — USC Keck School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/usc-keck-school-of-medicine/dominic-carusillo/) (MS1, 2018): Dominic treats school like a full-time job, studying from morning into the evening with webcast lectures and third-party resources like Pathoma for efficiency. Dominic considers webcast lectures and a strong relationship with a large hospital the most important things to look for in a school, and found shadowing the most valuable extracurricular, with attendings eager to show students their work. The area right around campus is economically struggling, but Dominic spends free time elsewhere in Los Angeles, which has plenty to do despite the traffic.
- [Guillaume Kugener — USC Keck School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/usc-keck-school-of-medicine/guillaume-kugener/) (MS4, 2023): Guillaume, a fourth-year headed into general surgery, says the best part of Keck is the time at LA County Hospital, where an under-resourced system gives medical students real responsibility and an up-close view of the social barriers patients face. A former computational biologist, Guillaume joined a lab after the first block to analyze surgical videos with deep learning, work that produced around 11 to 12 papers during medical school. Guillaume describes a preclinical phase of about a year and a half with few in-person requirements, and notes that a car is a must at the USC Health Sciences campus.
- [Sam Teles — USC Keck School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/usc-keck-school-of-medicine/sam-teles/) (MS1, 2018): Sam studies with Zanki flashcards and webcast lectures, which most of the class watches instead of attending, along with detailed notes the lecturers write for each lecture. Seeing patients at LA County, one of three hospitals on campus with Keck Hospital and Norris Cancer Center, is what Sam values most, because patients there are grateful for someone who listens. Sam is in the Health, Technology and Engineering program, which pairs medical students with engineering PhD students to work on health care innovation, and shares a method for finding out-of-state schools that actually admit out-of-state applicants.
- [Brian James — USF Health Morsani College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/morsani-college-of-medicine/brian-james/) (MS2, 2018): Brian describes four morning lectures, a weekly anatomy lab and a Doctoring course in downtown Tampa that teaches patient interviews and physical exams; lectures are recorded and only about a quarter of the class attends in person. USF’s Scholarly Concentrations put students in one of 11 tracks, such as law, business or nutrition and medicine, and a separate SELECT program focuses on leadership. Brian found faculty quick to act on feedback, and loves Tampa’s sports, nightlife and nearby beaches.
- [Chetna Thawani — USF Health Morsani College of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/morsani-college-of-medicine/chetna-thawani/) (MS2, 2019): Chetna describes USF’s Collegias, learning communities that group students for anatomy lab and doctoring, compete in inter-Collegia events and each have their own career adviser. A student board regularly brings the class’s feedback on lecturers and exams to faculty, who act on it, and the Doctoring course gives plenty of practice with standardized patients, including simulations with pharmacy and physical therapy students. Chetna, one of the youngest in the class, regrets skipping a gap year and is candid about feeling close to burnout.
- [Chris — VCU School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/virginia-commonwealth-university/chris/) (MS2, 2018): Chris watches lectures in the morning, builds study guides and flow charts to tell similar diseases apart, and attends required afternoon classes about twice a week; about a third of the class attends lecture regularly. Starting early in second year, students can join clinicians on house calls around Richmond to see patients who cannot get to a clinic, which showed Chris how much care has to adapt to patients’ finances, literacy and transportation. Chris loves Richmond’s history, took a gap year working as an EMT, and wishes anatomy were an admissions requirement.
- [Nik — Wayne State University School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/wayne-state-school-of-medicine/nik/) (MS1, 2018): Nik describes four lectures a day plus anatomy reviews, followed by long evenings reviewing with class notes, Boards and Beyond, BRS questions and Firecracker for spaced repetition. Wayne State’s student body is very diverse, which Nik credits for an open, relaxed environment, and the class of about 300 holds its parties in downtown Detroit. Clinical Skills sessions use standardized patients, with feedback from a classmate, the patient and a fourth-year student, and Nik, who struggled in the first weeks, credits asking for help with turning things around.
- [Annie Yau — Weill Cornell Medical College](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/weill-cornell-medical-college/annie-yau/) (MS1, 2018): Annie describes mornings of problem-based learning, small groups or lecture until 1pm, and afternoons for anatomy, preceptorship, electives or study, with plenty of downtime in first year for shadowing and the student-run free clinic. With just over 100 students, most of whom live in the same building in first year, the class is tight-knit, and pass/fail grading keeps stress down. Weill Cornell’s ties with Memorial Sloan Kettering, Rockefeller University and Hospital for Special Surgery bring abundant research and clinical opportunities, and New York keeps life exciting, from museums to discounted shows.
- [Chuck Chan — Western University College of Osteopathic Medicine of the Pacific](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/western-university-osteopathic/chuck-chan/) (OMS1, 2018): Chuck describes four to eight hours of class a day, including weekly sessions on patient encounters and OMM, with most students webcasting lectures and focusing on high-yield material. Chuck is in the Lifestyle Medicine track, which covers diet and physical and mental health, and values about eight standardized patient encounters each semester, including a psychiatry-focused OSCE. Chuck is candid about Pomona’s limited food options, crime and homelessness, and about how hard the lack of weekends and breaks can be.
- [Hadrian Mendoza — Yale School of Medicine](https://www.docstory.org/interviews/yale-school-of-medicine/hadrian-mendoza/) (MS2, 2018): Hadrian skips lecture and studies independently from late morning into the night, relying on Boards and Beyond, Pathoma, Sketchy and Anki. Yale’s pass/fail grading, with no ranking or AOA, supports what Hadrian calls a “gunner-free zone” of independent students; Hadrian directs a jazz band that rehearses weekly. In first year every student joins an interprofessional team with PA and nursing students that spends a half-day in clinic each week, and New Haven is a walkable college town with easy trains to New York and Boston.
